question: Using the WHO IMNCI classification for pneumonia, which of the following correctly matches age group to the fast-breathing threshold requiring classification as 'pneumonia' (non-severe)?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: These thresholds are REVERSED. Infants aged 2–12 months have a higher normal respiratory rate, so the IMNCI fast-breathing threshold is HIGHER (≥50/min). Older children aged 12 months–5 years have a lower threshold of ≥40/min. Getting this reversed leads to under-triage of sick infants and over-triage of older toddlers.

Correct. WHO IMNCI thresholds for fast breathing: 0–2 months ≥60/min (neonates), 2–12 months ≥50/min (infants), 12 months–5 years ≥40/min (young children). These age-specific cut-offs account for normally higher respiratory rates in younger infants. Any child meeting these thresholds with cough or difficulty breathing is classified as 'pneumonia' and requires oral amoxicillin.

A single threshold for all ages under 5 years is incorrect and dangerous. A rate of 40/min in a 3-month-old is normal (and would miss pneumonia), while in a 2-year-old it indicates fast breathing. IMNCI uses three age-specific thresholds: ≥60/min (0–2 months), ≥50/min (2–12 months), ≥40/min (12 months–5 years).

≥60/min is the IMNCI fast-breathing threshold for the youngest age group (0–2 months/neonates), not for infants 2–12 months. For 2–12 months the threshold is ≥50/min; for 12 months–5 years it is ≥40/min. Applying the neonatal threshold to infants would significantly under-diagnose pneumonia in this vulnerable age group.

overallFeedback.feedback: WHO IMNCI fast-breathing thresholds (must memorise): 0–2 months ≥60/min; 2–12 months ≥50/min; 12 months–5 years ≥40/min. Higher threshold for younger infants because their normal respiratory rates are higher.

Well done. Memorise these three IMNCI thresholds: 0–2 months ≥60/min, 2–12 months ≥50/min, 12 months–5 years ≥40/min. They define fast breathing and trigger the 'pneumonia' classification requiring treatment.
